missions/pentecostal-mission/name: Azusa Street and the Pentecostal missionary explosion (Garr, Assemblies of God, global Pentecostalism)
missions/pentecostal-mission/statusNote: Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity is the fastest-growing form of Christianity of the past century; the World Christian Database estimates well over 600 million adherents in the 2020s, though totals depend heavily on how ‘charismatic’ is defined. Most adherents live in Africa, Latin America and Asia and belong to nationally founded churches rather than missions.
missions/pentecostal-mission/summary: Beginning with Charles Parham’s Bible school in Topeka (1901) and William J. Seymour’s Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles (1906–09), Pentecostals taught that Spirit baptism, evidenced by speaking in tongues, empowered believers for world evangelisation before Christ’s imminent return. Within a few years missionaries had gone from Azusa Street and its satellite revivals to India, China, Africa, Scandinavia and South America, and the Assemblies of God (1914) built one of the largest mission organisations of the century. The movement’s later explosive growth was driven above all by indigenous preachers.
missions/pentecostal-mission/story:
Pentecostalism was missionary from the start. At Charles Fox Parham’s Bethel Bible School in Topeka, Kansas, Agnes Ozman spoke in tongues on 1 January 1901, and Parham taught that this gift was xenolalia — real foreign languages bestowed so that missionaries could preach abroad without study. In Houston in 1905 Parham’s segregated classes were attended, from the corridor, by William J. Seymour, an African American holiness preacher. Seymour carried the message to Los Angeles, and from April 1906 the Apostolic Faith Mission at 312 Azusa Street drew black, white, Latino and Asian worshippers in meetings that ran almost continuously until about 1909. Its paper, The Apostolic Faith, sent free to tens of thousands of readers, reported that ‘Pentecost has come’ and announced missionaries leaving for the ends of the earth.

The first wave of ‘missionaries of the one-way ticket’ left within months. Alfred G. Garr and Lillian Garr, believing they had received Bengali and Chinese, sailed for India and reached Calcutta at the end of 1906; finding that their tongues were not intelligible, they preached in English among missionaries and Anglo-Indians, helped spread Pentecostal experience in missionary circles, and went on to Hong Kong in 1907. Others went to Liberia, Angola and China. The disappointment of xenolalia led most Pentecostals to reinterpret tongues as prayer languages, but the conviction of empowerment for mission remained. Revivals elsewhere — the Welsh revival (1904–05), Pandita Ramabai’s Mukti Mission near Pune (1905), and the Korean revival (1907) — showed that the movement had multiple origins.

The experience spread by networks of holiness and evangelical periodicals. The Methodist Thomas Ball Barratt, having received Spirit baptism in New York, brought it to Kristiania (Oslo) in December 1906, and from there it reached Sweden (Lewi Pethrus’s Filadelfia church, Stockholm), Britain (Alexander Boddy in Sunderland, 1907) and Germany. Swedish Baptists Daniel Berg and Gunnar Vingren, influenced in Chicago by William Durham, landed at Belém in November 1910; their split from the local Baptist church in 1911 began what became the Assembleias de Deus, now Brazil’s largest Protestant church. Willis Hoover’s Methodist congregation in Valparaíso experienced revival in 1909, producing the Methodist Pentecostal Church of Chile. In South Africa John G. Lake and Thomas Hezmalhalch founded the Apostolic Faith Mission in 1908, whose Zionist offshoots fed into African independent churches.

Organisation followed. The Church of God in Christ (C. H. Mason, 1907) and the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) became Pentecostal; the Assemblies of God was founded at Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1914, with a strong emphasis on foreign missions, and adopted Roland Allen-style ‘indigenous church’ principles, systematised by Melvin Hodges in The Indigenous Church (1953). The Oneness controversy split the movement in 1916, and racial division hardened: the Assemblies of God was overwhelmingly white, and the Pentecostal Fellowship of North America (1948) excluded black churches until its dissolution and replacement in the ‘Memphis Miracle’ of 1994. British Pentecostals formed the Elim (1915) and Assemblies of God (1924) churches, with missions in Africa and India.

After 1945 the decisive growth came from national leaders and churches: the Church of Pentecost in Ghana (from James McKeown’s work, 1937), the Redeemed Christian Church of God (Nigeria, 1952), David Yonggi Cho’s Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul (1958), the Indian Pentecostal Church of God (1924) and Ceylon Pentecostal Mission, and Chinese house churches with strongly charismatic practice. Healing evangelists such as T. L. Osborn and Reinhard Bonnke drew vast crowds in Africa, while the charismatic renewal from 1960 carried Pentecostal experience into the historic Protestant and Catholic churches. Neo-Pentecostal megachurches, often teaching prosperity, multiplied in Latin America and Africa from the 1980s.

Scholars such as Allan Anderson and Walter Hollenweger argue that Pentecostalism’s growth owes most to its oral, participatory worship, its translation of the gospel into local idioms of spiritual power, healing and deliverance, and its openness to lay and women preachers. Critics point to the prosperity gospel, authoritarian ‘big man’ leadership, financial scandals, witchcraft accusations in deliverance ministries, and political alliances with strongmen. The movement now sends missionaries from Brazil, Nigeria, Korea and elsewhere throughout the world.
missions/pentecostal-mission/beliefs/0: Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, classically evidenced by speaking in tongues (the ‘initial evidence’ doctrine)
missions/pentecostal-mission/beliefs/1: The ‘full gospel’: Jesus as saviour, sanctifier (in holiness Pentecostalism), Spirit-baptiser, healer and coming king
missions/pentecostal-mission/beliefs/2: Divine healing and other spiritual gifts (prophecy, deliverance, miracles) as signs accompanying the preaching of the gospel
missions/pentecostal-mission/beliefs/3: Urgent premillennial expectation of Christ’s return, making world evangelisation the task of the ‘latter rain’
missions/pentecostal-mission/beliefs/4: Early belief that tongues were missionary languages (xenolalia), later reinterpreted as prayer and worship
missions/pentecostal-mission/beliefs/5: Priesthood of all believers expressed in lay, women’s and young people’s ministry, though institutional churches later restricted women’s leadership
missions/pentecostal-mission/strategies/: Independent ‘one-way ticket’ missionaries with little training or support, trusting divine provision
Spread through periodicals (The Apostolic Faith, Confidence, The Pentecostal Evangel) and networks of holiness missions
Healing campaigns and mass crusades emphasising signs and wonders
Indigenous-church principles: rapid training of national pastors and self-supporting churches (Hodges, AG Bible schools)
Lay evangelism by converts, open-air preaching and church planting in urban peripheries
Use of radio, television and later social media by national ministries
missions/pentecostal-mission/groupsReach: Working-class and migrant communities in the United States, including African Americans and Mexican Americans
The urban poor of Brazil, Chile, Guatemala and other Latin American countries
West African and southern African urban populations, through national churches and independent ministries
Dalit and tribal communities in Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Northeast India
Rural and urban believers in Korea, the Philippines, Indonesia and China
Members of mainline and Catholic churches through the charismatic renewal
missions/pentecostal-mission/challenges/: Failure of xenolalia and lack of training left early missionaries stranded, sick or returning home
Doctrinal splits: finished-work vs holiness sanctification (1910s), the Oneness controversy (1916)
Racial segregation within the American movement
Opposition from holiness and fundamentalist leaders who called tongues demonic or delusional
Persecution by Catholic authorities in Latin America and state restrictions in China and elsewhere
Fragmentation into thousands of independent churches and ministries with weak accountability
missions/pentecostal-mission/harms/0: Racial division after the interracial beginnings at Azusa Street, institutionalised in white-only fellowships until 1994
missions/pentecostal-mission/harms/1: Prosperity teaching that links giving to wealth and health has been criticised for exploiting poor congregations
missions/pentecostal-mission/harms/2: Deliverance and witchcraft-accusation practices in some African churches have contributed to the abuse of children and elderly people
missions/pentecostal-mission/harms/3: Financial and sexual scandals among televangelists and megachurch leaders
missions/pentecostal-mission/harms/4: Denunciation of traditional religions and of other churches, sometimes provoking conflict
missions/pentecostal-mission/harms/5: Authoritarian leadership cultures and alliances with authoritarian politicians in parts of Africa and Latin America
missions/pentecostal-mission/development: Made Christianity a mass religion of the poor in Latin America and accelerated church growth in Africa and Asia
Opened leadership to lay people, the uneducated and (especially early) women
Created vigorous indigenous churches largely independent of Western control
Influenced all major traditions through the charismatic renewal, including Catholicism
Developed social ministries in education, rehabilitation and community development (documented by Miller and Yamamori)
Turned the global South into a major sender of missionaries
missions/pentecostal-mission/outcome: Pentecostalism became the second-largest Christian grouping after Catholicism by many estimates, centred in the global South. Its missionary dynamism shifted from Western mission boards to national churches and transnational networks, carrying both renewal and controversy.

Tongues as initial evidence and as missionary xenolalia
Discredited by scandal in 1907; his teaching shaped the movement
missions/pentecostal-mission/keyPeople/1: Pastor of the Azusa Street Mission
His mission became the movement’s symbolic centre
missions/pentecostal-mission/keyPeople/2: First Azusa Street missionary to Asia
Spread Pentecostal experience among missionaries; abandoned xenolalia theory
missions/pentecostal-mission/keyPeople/3: Methodist minister and Pentecostal pioneer in Europe
Seeded Pentecostalism in Scandinavia, Britain and Germany
missions/pentecostal-mission/keyPeople/4: Co-founder of the Assembleias de Deus
Brazilian AG grew into the country’s largest Protestant church
missions/pentecostal-mission/keyPeople/5: Co-founder of the Assembleias de Deus
Supported the work as a foundry worker and colporteur
missions/pentecostal-mission/keyPeople/6: Expelled by Methodists; founded the Methodist Pentecostal Church of Chile
missions/pentecostal-mission/keyPeople/7: Founder of Yoido Full Gospel Church
Built the world’s largest congregation; later convicted of embezzlement (2014)
missions/pentecostal-mission/countries/0: Topeka (1901) and Azusa Street (1906) launched the movement; the Assemblies of God (1914) became a major sending body.
missions/pentecostal-mission/countries/1: The Garrs arrived in Calcutta; Mukti revival (1905) and Kerala churches (IPC, 1924; Ceylon Pentecostal Mission) built an indigenous movement.
missions/pentecostal-mission/countries/2: T. B. Barratt’s meetings in Kristiania made Oslo the gateway of European Pentecostalism.
missions/pentecostal-mission/countries/3: Azusa missionaries and the Garrs worked in Hong Kong and south China; later indigenous groups (True Jesus Church, Jesus Family) and house churches adopted charismatic practice.
missions/pentecostal-mission/countries/4: Alexander Boddy’s Sunderland conventions; Elim (1915) and Assemblies of God (1924) sent missionaries to Africa and India.
missions/pentecostal-mission/countries/5: John G. Lake founded the Apostolic Faith Mission, whose Zionist offshoots influenced African independent churches.
missions/pentecostal-mission/countries/6: The Valparaíso revival produced the Methodist Pentecostal Church, an early fully national Pentecostal church.
missions/pentecostal-mission/countries/7: Berg and Vingren founded the Assembleias de Deus in Belém; Brazil became the largest Pentecostal country.
missions/pentecostal-mission/countries/8: James McKeown’s work led to the Church of Pentecost, now a major sending church.
missions/pentecostal-mission/countries/9: The Redeemed Christian Church of God and other national churches grew into transnational networks.
missions/pentecostal-mission/countries/1: Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul grew to several hundred thousand members.

Pentecostalism began among missionaries and converts of the Primitive Methodist mission in the 1930s and grew rapidly from the 1960s; by the 2000s Protestants, most of them Pentecostal, were a large minority.
missions/pentecostal-mission/journeys/0/: The Garrs from Azusa Street to Calcutta and Hong Kong

Expecting to preach in Bengali by miraculous gift, the Garrs found they could not; they ministered in English in Calcutta and then moved to Hong Kong, spreading Pentecostal experience among missionaries.
missions/pentecostal-mission/journeys/1/: Barratt received Spirit baptism in New York while fund-raising, and his December 1906 meetings in Oslo spread the movement through northern Europe.
missions/pentecostal-mission/journeys/2/: Following a prophecy naming ‘Pará’, the two Swedes sailed from New York and arrived in Belém in November 1910, founding the Assembleias de Deus the next year.
missions/pentecostal-mission/journeys/3/: John G. Lake to South Africa
John G. Lake and Thomas Hezmalhalch
Lake’s party drew on Zionist networks already in South Africa and founded the Apostolic Faith Mission.
missions/pentecostal-mission/relations/0: Chilean and Brazilian Pentecostal churches became the core of Latin American Protestant growth.
missions/pentecostal-mission/relations/1: Apostolic Faith Mission and Pentecostal ideas shaped Zionist and Aladura churches, though these also had independent origins.
missions/pentecostal-mission/relations/2: Korean Pentecostalism, especially Yoido Full Gospel Church, became a major engine of Korean missions.
missions/pentecostal-mission/relations/3: Pentecostal churches in Nigeria, Brazil and Ghana became leading majority-world sending bodies.
missions/pentecostal-mission/agreements/: Shared the holiness pattern of a post-conversion crisis experience and lay, women’s and working-class ministry.
Pentecostals increasingly joined evangelical bodies (NAE, 1942; Lausanne) and shared their priority on evangelism.
missions/pentecostal-mission/disagreemen: Many fundamentalist and faith-mission leaders were cessationists who held that tongues and miracles had ceased with the apostles, and condemned Pentecostalism.
Most Pentecostals stayed outside the WCC and distrusted its theology, although some (e.g. Chilean churches, 1961) joined and dialogue began from the 1970s.

Church Growth writers studied Pentecostal growth admiringly, but Pentecostals disputed managerial, numerical approaches that downplayed the Spirit’s sovereignty — a gap partly closed by Wagner’s turn to ‘signs and wonders’.
missions/pentecostal-mission/deviations/: The early xenolalia doctrine proved false and was quietly abandoned
The interracial, egalitarian vision of Azusa Street gave way within a decade to segregated denominations
Prosperity teaching departed from the early movement’s ascetic, other-worldly holiness piety
Restrictions on women’s ordination in many institutional Pentecostal churches reversed early practice
